I guess what I've seen from Chinese laser capacity expansion: 

1. Dongshan/Source Photonics (索尔思): 9M/month capacity -> 22M/month Q4 ->  300m/year in 2027 (mostly EML, but blended)

Claims of 1B/year "target" for laser chips with no deadline, but I'd take this as a grain of salt. 

2. Shijia (仕佳): 72M/year for 100mW CW, 2-3 year project (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

3. Yunling (云岭): 18.75M/year 70/100mW CW, 3 year schedule (mainly 2029 full capacity online)

4. Ligent (纳真), some reports stated 170M target for total capacity (also blended, lot of which is 200G EML)

5. Yuanjie: ~10M/year currently, expanding for early 2027 and 2028, but no quantities. 

6. Hongchen: I think this was the perfect example of flooding H2 2026 arguments. With some some optical bears claiming 60-70M capacity...

But this turned out to completely wrong... Their actual statements were "70/100 mW products are entering small-volume production". 

7. Dingxin Optoelectronics - Targeting 15M/year blended (with 70/100mW CW and 100G EML lines)

Obviously mapped many others like Everbright/Accelink and did some guesses around laser mixes, but only included public disclosures. 

From your pluggable vendor channel checks: 

- 70mW/100mW lasers are actually a bottleneck right now per Innolight/Cambridge channel checks, laser ASPs actually increasing. 

Lasers are tighter than they were a few months ago. 

I don't think there's a giant moat here, Chinese players are already competitive. But a bottleneck is a bottleneck, and anyone with capacity to monetize that will benefit, since it's a volume game. 

In terms of what the larger pluggable makers are actually doing: 

- Innolight September disclosure: actively introducing new suppliers and are planning to sign 2-3 year-long contracts to lock upstream capacity for lasers (still actively securing supply for 1.6T pluggables)

So there's some game theory over who can lock up qualified capacity among all your players. 

Even if there's some over-ordering, laser BOM is cheap, so they'd probably want to lock up capacity with more suppliers than lose billions in downstream revenue. (also kinda hurts competitors) 

- High end lines (for CPO), non-competitive with Western players like $LITE / $COHR as of next few years. But Chinese players would eventually develop the technology. 

- $AAOI CEO: Chinese suppliers several years behind on high-power CPO/DWDM laser production "not in the next 2,3 years"

- $LITE CEO questioned whether claimed Chinese manufacturing capacity was translating into commercial output. "At least at the moment, we see no impact from any Chinese laser supply."

This is despite Shijia, Everbright, Yuanjie and others stating 400mW capabilities and capacity expansion targets from Chinese companies. Although Western CEOs might be disputing their reliability and capability to scale these lines. 

I see lower end range bottleneck for pluggable will gradually ease as more capacity comes online 2028. But all evidence points against near-term overflooding. 

The 100mW range for example, someone cited 2 years of equipment investment. Higher ranges were 3 years for equipment investment? So even some Chinese players take years for capacity to come online. 

The multi year laser shortage statements from laser company executives seems to be true... especially among higher end ranges, since buildout takes a lot of time. 

Legitimate competition coming from China, but as of now there's a scramble for CW LTAs among the industry in 2026-2027. 

Lot of capacity is probably allocated toward higher spec lasers or EML, as seen with EML bottlenecking $LITE for the longest time (they have more supply now) that they had to buy CW off the market instead of supplying it themselves. 

This is while tail end for 800G demand for example, might continue much much longer than expected with sovereign DC buildouts. So there might be some surprising dynamics for duration, we'll see.

In the end I do think supply chains will be bifurcated: 

- Chinese players will prioritize domestic capabilities but heavily sources globally. 

- Western players (now) prioritize Western supply chains unless China comes online with cheap enough supply (which don't see happening near-term). 

TLDR: 
-> Multi-year shortage definitely seems accurate for higher end specs
-> Lot of China capacity overflooding claims earlier from H1 turned out to be completely false. People keep making them for some reason across memory to photonics. 
-> Chinese laser players are competitive for 70mW/100MW, meaningful expansion Y/Y, but nothing showing overflooding, given laser demand increasing, probably gradual easing into 2028. 

We'll see, supply chain evolves month after month, just my current opinion from what I'm seeing.

CSPs and AI labs: CSPs and AI labs had requested the development of lower-stack HBM products, such as 4-high and 6-high configurations, for use in low-end inference products. Those plans now appear to have been shelved, with 8-high once again emerging as the minimum stack height.

NVIDIA: Rubin’s specifications have changed amid base die supply constraints and requests from customers prioritizing bandwidth over cost efficiency. The original plan called for a mix of 8-high and 12-high HBM, but the 8-high option appears to have been dropped. For Rubin Ultra, scheduled for release in 2027, multiple architectural variants are currently undergoing tape-out. Initial versions are expected to use the highest-specification 8-high HBM4, while subsequent versions are expected to adopt either 8-high or 12-high HBM4E.

AMD: AMD is expected to use a mix of 8-high and 12-high HBM4 in its 2027 products. One notable development is the upcoming MI450, which is expected to increase the number of HBM stacks within the CoWoS package to 12, delivering 288GB of HBM4. The increase from eight to 12 HBM stacks per CoWoS package is a positive development for HBM content over the medium to long term.

OpenAI and Anthropic: OpenAI is expected to adopt 12-high HBM4, while Anthropic is expected to use 8-high HBM4.

This chart is an oversimplification, but it’s the core of why I’m not selling, even at these levels.

Since January 2025, the SOX is up about 114%. Forward earnings for the same index are up roughly 198%. 

Earnings nearly tripled while prices only doubled, so semis are cheaper today on forward earnings than they were at the start of 2025.

So what changed in the last 20 days? The cost of the buildout went up. 

Oil above $100, inflation back at 3.7%, a 10-year above 5% and junk spreads blowing out on the most leveraged builders all make every data center more expensive to finance. Meanwhile the demand signals haven’t cracked, and GPU rental prices just hit a record.

 The war keeps oil high, oil keeps inflation sticky, sticky inflation keeps rates up, and high rates compress what the market will pay for growth. 

End the war, and that whole chain runs in reverse.

That’s the difference between this artificial problem and a real demand problem.

The selloff continues. Next, I’m shifting from shorting beta to shorting alpha. I call it the “reverse bottleneck trade”—the counterpart to the earlier bottleneck trade.

The logic is simple: AI demand will keep growing, but that growth may slow, while upstream suppliers keep expanding capacity in response to shortages and fat margins. Once effective supply catches up with demand, bargaining power shifts back downstream. During a shortage, customers care first about availability. Good enough will do. Once supply is plentiful, they start comparing performance, cost, power consumption, and reliability again. That’s when we find out who wins orders on competitiveness and who was simply picking up overflow because the leaders couldn’t supply enough.

My watchlist includes memory runner-up MU, second- and third-tier optical players COHR and AAOI, and foundry runner-up INTC.

This trade doesn’t even require the AI bubble to burst. Supply growth just needs to start outpacing demand growth. I think there’s a very high probability these stocks put in an “Everest chart” over the next year—a towering peak followed by a collapse back down. If you don’t have the stomach to go all-in on outright shorts, anti-bottleneck pair trades are another good way to express the view: long LITE / short AAOI; long TSM / short INTC; long NVDA / short AMD or AVGO.

- data volume is compounding across every industry (including healthcare records, imaging, and claims)

- AI requires continuous research, not just implementation.

- connectivity permanently expands the attack surface - Information security analysts grow because the cost of being unsecured keeps rising; especially in healthcare, finance, and critical infrastructure

- solar and wind appear because of the energy transition, but the absolute job numbers remain small compared with healthcare and tech.

**焦点**｜全日最大单一跌幅来自燃料电池股 BE ，大泻11.24%，主因为前一交易日盘后公布的业绩；存储股 WDC 同样于前一交易日盘后交卷，今日收跌2.97%，两者的波动均为财报后的直接反应。至于跌幅榜第二位的 CRDO ，并非财报日,其9.51%的急泻与同属半导体链的 SMTC 升5.50%形成尖锐对照，反映资金并非整体撤离AI硬件,而是在链条内部高度拣择、强弱互换。另一值得注意的是网安三股同日录得逾7%的齐升——在61只下跌的淡市中,这类集体性的板块级跳升,通常意味着板块资金配置的切换,而非个股消息驱动。

**小结**｜全日格局是典型的「指数平稳、内部分化」：纳指近乎平收,道指却跌逾1.2%,旧经济权重与科网龙头的裂口再度扩阔,而市宽（45升61跌）更接近市场的真实温度。分析指,标普失守760关后,此位将由支持转为阻力,而纳指能否守住700关,仍是短线强弱的关键位;若权重科网的升势无法扩散至市宽,目前由少数板块撑起的指数结构将难以持久。与此同时,AI产业链的财富分配问题亦值得留意——本轮周期中最具爆发力的资产大多留在一级市场,公开市场投资者所能拣择的,只剩链条中强弱悬殊的二线标的,这或正是今日 SMTC 与 CRDO 分道扬镳的更深层背景。

我发现这轮AI最狠的地方不是估值，是上车那道门早就关了。微软1986年上市的时候市值才几亿美金，亚马逊97年上市四亿多，后面那几千倍是在公开市场里涨出来的，散户想买随时买。OpenAI现在一级市场估值已经五千亿往上，等它哪天真上市，前面那一千倍早就被十几家crossover基金和主权基金分完了。所以每次有人问「AI泡沫破了散户怎么办」，我觉得这问题问歪了——这次散户压根没买到泡沫，手里能拿的就是卖铲子的那几家，NVDA和存储，钱是当季就进账的。真要破，亏的是中东的主权基金、几个大学捐赠基金，还有你养老金账户里那笔你看不到净值、也赎不回来的PE份额。假设你是加州一个中学老师，你的退休金通过某只基金间接持了一点OpenAI，你不知道占多少，也没人问过你一句🌚
